subject.title: The Evening-Watch: A Dialogue
subject.author: Henry Vaughan
subject.text:
BODY

Farewell! I go to sleep; but when
The day-star springs, I'll wake again.

SOUL

Go, sleep in peace; and when thou liest
Unnumber'd in thy dust, when all this frame
Is but one dram, and what thou now descriest
In sev'ral parts shall want a name,
Then may his peace be with thee, and each dust
Writ in his book, who ne'er betray'd man's trust!

BODY

Amen! but hark, ere we two stray
How many hours dost think 'till day?

SOUL

Ah go; th'art weak, and sleepy. Heav'n
Is a plain watch, and without figures winds
All ages up; who drew this circle, even
He fills it; days and hours are blinds.
Yet this take with thee. The last gasp of time
Is thy first breath, and man's eternal prime.

title: Two Questions Vaughan's Soul Refuses to Answer
standfirst: Twice in this small dialogue the Body asks its Soul a plain question about time, and twice the Soul answers something else entirely. Vaughan wrote it not long after his brother's death and an illness he later described, in his own hand, as a near miss with dying.

sections.heading: A Question Asked Twice, Answered Neither Time
sections.body:
The Body speaks first, and it speaks like someone who has already made up their mind: "Farewell! I go to sleep; but when / The day-star springs, I'll wake again." Two lines, one rhymed couplet, a plain future tense. It isn't a question. It's a plan.

The plan survives one exchange. When the Body does finally ask something concrete — "How many hours dost think 'till day?" — the Soul spends six lines answering without once mentioning hours. Its first reply had already talked about dust, about the parts of a person that "shall want a name" once death is finished with them, about a peace that arrives in place of a wake-up call. Ask this Soul what time it is and it tells you about eternity instead.

That mismatch is the whole poem, working in miniature. The Body speaks in couplets — four beats, rhymed in twos, shut as fast as they open. The Soul answers in six-line stanzas that take three times as long to finish. A small, practical question gets an answer built on a scale the question never asked for.

sections.heading: A Watch With Nothing Written On Its Face
sections.body:
By the second exchange the Body has stopped planning and started worrying, which is presumably why it finally asks something as ordinary as the time. The Soul's answer builds an image that does the refusing for it:

> Heav'n
> Is a plain watch, and without figures winds
> All ages up; who drew this circle, even
> He fills it; days and hours are blinds.

A watch, in the ordinary sense, is read by looking at the figures marked round its face and doing arithmetic against them — three hours gone, five still to run. Heaven's watch, the Soul says, has no figures on it. It still winds. It still turns on a circle, the way any watch mechanism does. But nobody consults it to find out how much time is left, because there is no "how much longer" left to find. Days and hours are blinds: screens put up to make time look like something that runs down, when what's actually turning underneath is a single unbroken circle someone else both drew and keeps full.

It is a strange object to hand a frightened person instead of an answer — not comfort exactly, but a redrawn instrument. Ask what time it is, and be told the face you're reading was never built for where you're going.

sections.heading: He Had Already Been the Body in This Dialogue
sections.body:
Henry Vaughan's younger brother, William, was born in 1628 and [died in 1648](https://englishhistory.net/poets/henry-vaughan/), not yet twenty — a loss biographers connect to the turn Vaughan's writing takes soon afterward, away from love poetry and satire and toward the devotional verse that became Silex Scintillans. Two years later, Vaughan himself fell seriously ill. He never named the disease. But in the preface he added to the book's second part in 1655, he did not treat it lightly, writing that he had been "[nigh unto death](https://archive.org/stream/silexscintillans00vaug/silexscintillans00vaug_djvu.txt), and am still at no great distance from it," and describing the crisis itself more starkly still: he had prepared himself for a message of death, and instead God had "[answer me with life](https://archive.org/stream/silexscintillans00vaug/silexscintillans00vaug_djvu.txt)."

That is not a writer reaching for a devotional figure of speech. It reads like a man describing a specific stretch of nights in which he had already done what the Body does at the start of "The Evening-Watch" — lain down uncertain whether he would get up again — and had, by his own account, come close to guessing wrong. He gives the Body its confident farewell, "I'll wake again." He keeps for the Soul the harder knowledge he had, apparently, just finished acquiring himself.

sections.heading: Two Pages Apart in the Same Book
sections.body:
In the first part of Silex Scintillans, printed in 1650, "The Evening-Watch: A Dialogue" follows directly on from "The Morning-Watch" — [page 83 to page 85](https://archive.org/stream/silexscintillans00vaug/silexscintillans00vaug_djvu.txt) in the table of contents of the original volume, with nothing printed between them. Vaughan built this stretch of the book out of a single day: waking, then sleeping, set back to back.

The two poems don't share a register. "The Morning-Watch" opens running: "[O joys! infinite sweetness](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/45428/the-morning-watch)! with what flow'rs / And shoots of glory my soul breaks and buds!" — and goes on to hear the whole created world as an instrument tuning itself, "the [great chime](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/45428/the-morning-watch) / And symphony of nature," where "Prayer is / The [world in tune](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/45428/the-morning-watch)." "The Evening-Watch" opens on a much smaller sound: two voices saying goodnight to each other. Waking, in this book, gets to shout. Sleep has to reason its way through instead.

Both titles lean on the old double sense of "watch" — a shift of duty kept through the night, and the biblical instruction to stay alert in prayer rather than drift into sleep unprepared. Vaughan wrote and revised both poems from Brecknockshire, the Usk valley he later took his pen-name from — he signed himself "[the Silurist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Vaughan)," after the Silures who once held that ground — and here he turns one unremarkable day into two watches kept, morning and evening, with the harder one given the shape of an argument rather than a shout.

sections.heading: The Least of a Dead Man's Converts
sections.body:
Vaughan named his own model outright. In the same 1655 preface, he credited George Herbert as the first English poet to make devotional verse actually work as poetry, writing that Herbert's holy life and verse had gained many pious converts, "of [whom I am the least](https://archive.org/stream/silexscintillans00vaug/silexscintillans00vaug_djvu.txt)." Herbert had died in 1633, when Vaughan was eleven; they never met. What Vaughan inherited wasn't friendship but a form. Herbert's own Temple contains poems built as exchanges between two voices arguing across a single short space — his "[A Dialogue-Antheme](https://www.ccel.org/h/herbert/temple/Dialogue.html)" stages Death boasting of having killed Christ, and a Christian speaker answering that the boast has already cost Death its own future. "The Evening-Watch" runs the same machine on smaller, more domestic material: not Death confronted by triumphant faith, but an ordinary bedtime exchange that turns out to be about the same thing.

It did not make Vaughan famous in his own lifetime. He spent most of his working years as a country physician in Brecknockshire, publishing almost nothing after 1655, and stayed a minor figure for two centuries. His wider recovery came later, when readers went looking for the poets standing behind Wordsworth and [found Vaughan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Vaughan) waiting under him, along with Tennyson and, later still, Siegfried Sassoon. He is usually filed as Herbert's student. "The Evening-Watch" is a fair place to see why that undersells him: it takes a form Herbert had used to stage triumph over Death in the abstract, and turns it, quietly, on the one night Vaughan had apparently just needed it for himself.
